authored.body_html:
What this is

This is the vaṃsa half of the chronicle genre — 569 of the roughly 1,060 witnesses in the chronicle genre, against 328 plain Tamnan and 159 Secular History. Vaṃsa means descent — a lineage, a line of transmission — and that is the organising idea: these texts answer the question how did this get here from there, where "this" is a relic, a teaching, an image, or the Buddha's dispensation itself.

It is the biggest single body of narrative prose in the archive, and the most recopied. 126 of the 569 titles name a ธาตุ — a relic or its stupa. That is the genre's centre of gravity, and it is a physical one.

The Buddha's life, and then everyone's death

The chronological spine starts before Lanna exists. Twenty witnesses carry some form of ปฐมสัมโพธิ, the Pathamasambodhi — the Buddha's biography from the Bodhisatta's descent to the awakening — and the three oldest are the oldest chronicle manuscripts in the entire archive: ms 4421 (1574), ms 4387 (1592) and ms 4635 (1592), all three copied at Wat Lai Hin Luang in Lampang. Whatever else was worth writing out in the north in the 1570s, the Buddha's life story was.

Then the shelf does something the canon does not: it tells you how everybody died. Twenty-five titles here name a นิพพาน, and at Wat Sung Men they form an obvious numbered set — fascicle by fascicle, saint by saint:

  • ms 1076 — มหากัสสะปนิพพาน ผูกต้น, Mahākassapa, "first fascicle"
  • ms 1077 — มหาอานันทะนิพพานวัตถุ ผูกถ้วนสี่, Ānanda, fourth
  • ms 1073 — Bakkula, fifth
  • ms 1080 — ทัพพเถรนิพพานวัตถุ ผูกถ้วนหก, Dabba, sixth
  • ms 1072 — พาหิยเถรนิพพานวัตถุ ผูกเจ็ด, Bāhiya, seventh
  • ms 1078 — อโสกธัมมราชนิพพานวัตถุ ผูกถ้วนแปด, King Asoka, eighth
  • ms 1075 — มหาโมคคะลานิพพานวัตถุ ผูกถ้วนสิบ, Moggallāna, tenth

with Sāriputta (ms 1074, 1850) and the Buddha's father Suddhodana (ms 1079) filed alongside, and — copied out on its own at Wat Sung Men in 1841 — ms 1984, นางยโสธรานิพพาน, the parinibbāna of Yasodharā, the wife the Bodhisatta left. (The series survived the cataloguing intact but not the labelling: the fifth and Sāriputta's were tagged Sutta and went to the canon shelf, while their neighbours in the same numbered run stayed here — a small, checkable example of how a genre boundary cuts through a work.) The set repeats elsewhere: ms 2743 at Wat Mueang Mo (1866) bundles four deaths into one leaf-bundle, and Yasodharā's own turns up at Wat Phra That Lampang Luang as early as 1728 (ms 4911).

Inference — a genre that files ten separate death-narratives as a numbered series is not doing hagiography by accident. It is building a chronicle of endings — the dispensation losing its people one by one, which is the necessary setup for the other half of the shelf.

Because the other half is the future. Fourteen witnesses of the อนาคตวงส์ — Anāgatavaṃsa, the chronicle of the Buddha still to come — sit here, three of them at Wat Chedi Luang in Chiang Mai (ms 4793, 1797; ms 4794, 1811; ms 4795, 1854), two at Wat Phra That Lampang Luang (ms 4824, 1697; ms 4833, 1770), one with a full Pali commentary attached (ms 1412, Pali amatarasadhārā ṭīkā anakatawong, Wat Sung Men, 1836). Read the shelf end to end and it is a single arc: the Buddha comes, the Buddha's people die, the teaching runs its five thousand years — 14 titles in the archive count that span out loud, ห้าพันวัสสา — and then Metteyya arrives. See Wat Chedi Luang.

The relics, and where the north put itself on the map

Between those two ends lies what the north actually cared about: which fragments of the body came here, and by what route.

  • ทันตธาตุ — the tooth-relic, 16 witnesses across the genre, at Wat Phra Sing (ms 51, 1761), Wat Na Pang in Nan (ms 654, 1793), and six or more times at Wat Sung Men (ms 2009, 1890; ms 2016, 1852; ms 2231, 1839; ms 2243, 1841). Also วามทันตธาตุ, the left tooth (ms 2433, 1837; ms 3517) — the tradition distinguishing which side of the jaw.
  • อุรังคธาตุ — the breast-bone relic, four witnesses, the earliest ms 778 at Wat Chiang Man (1799) and ms 226 at Wat Phra That Chang Kham in Nan (1820), filed as นิทาน, a tale. This is the chronicle of Phra That Phanom on the Mekong — the Lao-side great relic, kept in Lanna libraries, and the archive holds four more titles naming ธาตุพนม directly.
  • ธาตุตะโค่ง — and here is the one worth stopping on. Eighteen witnesses, and two of them (ms 783, ms 791 at Wat Chiang Man) give the full name: สิงคุตตรธาตุตะโค่ง, the relic of Siṅguttara hill — which is the Shwedagon, in Yangon. Northern Thai monks copied the chronicle of a Burmese pagoda eighteen times, at Wat Sung Men, at Wat Lai Hin Luang, at Wat Phra Luang, the earliest dated 1740 (ms 2364). And ms 6682, at Wat Ratanaram in 1871, is titled ตำนานดอยทุงก่ายเขาทะโค่ง — the tamnan of Doi Tung set against Takong hill. Inference — that is a claim, not a courtesy: the north measuring its own relic mountain against the greatest reliquary in the region. Relic chronicles are how polities argued about rank.
  • ธาตุห้าหลัง, the five reliquaries; เกสาธาตุ, the hair; พระบาท, the footprint — each with its own small literature, and each pinned to a place you can still walk to. The atlas and the wats are the right companions to this shelf.

Threading them all together is พระเจ้าเลียบโลก — the Buddha's walking tour of the north — with 13 of its 16 witnesses filed here, and มูลสาสนา, the Mūlasāsanā, the chronicle of how the ordination lineage itself arrived, in four copies (ms 793 at Wat Chiang Man; ms 2545 at Wat Sung Men; ms 5395, Wat Ban Luk, 1908; ms 6637, 1834).

The Sinhalese ancestry is on the shelf too, not merely implied: seven copies of the ถูปวงส์ (Thūpavaṃsa, Ceylon's chronicle of the stupa) sit here — the earliest ms 5030 at Wat Ban Ueam, Lampang, 1715 — alongside the มหาวงส์ (ms 639, Wat Na Pang, Nan, 1813; ms 3407, 1881). The Lanna vaṃsa was built on a Sri Lankan model and the model is filed beside the copies.

Ten titles are วัตถุ tales — Mae na kotami watthu, Mokkalan watthu, Cotika thela watthu — story-cases attached to a doctrinal point, where this sub-genre shades toward the jātaka; ten more are ฏีกา commentary, where it shades toward the canon proper.

The shape of the collection

Physically canonical — 92% palm-leaf (525 of 569, plus 28 on mulberry paper and 2 on khoi) — and well-dated: 376 witnesses carry a date, spanning 1574–1990, one of the longest runs in the archive.

But the geography is markedly more spread than the scholastic genres, across 80 named temples. Phrae leads (176), but Phayao (90), Chiang Mai (78) and Lampang (73) all hold substantial shares, with Lamphun (32), Nan (31), Mae Hong Son (30) and Chiang Rai (27) behind. At temple level Wat Sung Men (128) is joined by Wat Si Khom Kham in Phayao (61), Wat Mueang Mo (26), Wat Lai Hin Luang (26) and Wat Chiang Man (21). Because each relic and each that generated its own chronicle where it stood, the vaṃsa material is distributed across the landscape of sacred sites rather than pooled in one library — the opposite of the canon's Wat Sung Men gravity.

Notes

  • Localised, and that is the value. The tamnan of a named that is a primary source for the history of that site and the polity around it. Site by site, this sub-genre is historically richer than its even palm-leaf profile suggests, and it rewards a finer pass shrine by shrine rather than a genre-level browse.
  • The Takong cluster is an unworked research thread. Eighteen copies of a Burmese relic chronicle in northern Thai libraries, from 1740 onward, one of them explicitly comparing Doi Tung to it. Inference — that is evidence about how Lanna located itself inside a wider Buddhist world, and it is sitting in plain sight in the title field.
  • Read beside its siblings. Where a chronicle supplies a polity's charter it also touches customary law — two manuscripts titled Tamnan Phanya Mangrai are filed on the law shelf, not this one. The Secular History and plain Tamnan halves are the obvious companions, and the Tamnan page explains why their counts must not simply be added to these.
  • Documentary, not efficacious — and entirely untranscribed. None of the 569 are flagged research-priority; the claim on attention is historical. But not one of them has a transcribed page in this archive. A single full Pathamasambodhi or Anāgatavaṃsa would be the largest single addition of narrative text the collection could receive.
